    <!-- Header -->
    <div class="guide-header">
        <h1>Clawdbot/Moltbot Security Guide</h1>
        <p style="color: var(--text-muted); font-size: 1.1rem;">The viral AI assistant with 30K+ stars - and
            hundreds of exposed instances granting root access</p>
        <div style="margin-top: 1rem; color: var(--text-muted);">

    <!-- Section 1: What is Clawdbot -->
    <section id="what-is-clawdbot">
        <h2><i class="fas fa-robot"></i> What is Clawdbot/Moltbot?</h2>

        <p>Clawdbot (now renamed <strong>Moltbot</strong>) is an open-source, self-hosted AI assistant that
            functions like a personal JARVIS for your digital life. Created by Peter Steinberger, it became one of
            the fastest-growing GitHub repositories ever, amassing nearly 30,000 stars within weeks of its release.
        </p>

        <p>Unlike cloud-based AI assistants like ChatGPT or Claude, Clawdbot runs entirely on your own
            infrastructure, giving you complete control over your data - but also complete responsibility for
            security.</p>

        <div class="info-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-lightbulb"></i> Key Distinction:</strong> Clawdbot is NOT the same as
            "ClaudeBot" (Anthropic's web crawler). Clawdbot is a personal AI assistant that was renamed to Moltbot
            after Anthropic raised trademark concerns.
        </div>

        <h3>Core Concept</h3>
        <p>Think of Clawdbot as an AI-powered command center that:</p>
        <ul>
            <li><i class="fas fa-check-circle" style="color: var(--accent-green);"></i> Runs locally on your machine
                or server</li>
            <li><i class="fas fa-check-circle" style="color: var(--accent-green);"></i> Integrates with your
                messaging apps (WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack, Discord, iMessage, Teams)</li>
            <li><i class="fas fa-check-circle" style="color: var(--accent-green);"></i> Executes shell commands on
                your behalf</li>
            <li><i class="fas fa-check-circle" style="color: var(--accent-green);"></i> Manages files and automates
                tasks</li>
            <li><i class="fas fa-check-circle" style="color: var(--accent-green);"></i> Controls your browser and
                web interactions</li>
            <li><i class="fas fa-check-circle" style="color: var(--accent-green);"></i> Sends proactive
                notifications and reminders</li>
        </ul>
    </section>

    <!-- Section 2: Timeline -->
    <section id="timeline">
        <h2><i class="fas fa-clock"></i> Timeline of Events</h2>

        <div class="timeline">
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <div class="timeline-date">Early January 2026</div>
                <p>Clawdbot is released as open-source. Rapid viral adoption begins with thousands of stars per day.
                </p>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <div class="timeline-date">Mid-January 2026</div>
                <p>Security researchers begin discovering hundreds of exposed Clawdbot instances on the public
                    internet with no authentication.</p>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <div class="timeline-date">January 27, 2026</div>
                <p>Project renamed from Clawdbot to <strong>Moltbot</strong> due to trademark concerns from
                    Anthropic (makers of Claude).</p>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <div class="timeline-date">Late January 2026</div>
                <p>Malicious VS Code extension "ClawdBot Agent" discovered dropping ScreenConnect malware. Real
                    attacks reported including email inbox wipes.</p>
            </div>
        </div>
    </section>

    <!-- Section 3: Capabilities -->
    <section id="capabilities">
        <h2><i class="fas fa-cogs"></i> Capabilities & Features</h2>

        <p>Understanding what Clawdbot can do is essential for understanding the security risks. The power that
            makes it attractive is exactly what makes it dangerous if misconfigured.</p>

        <table class="comparison-table">
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Capability</th>
                    <th>Description</th>
                    <th>Security Implication</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Shell Access</strong></td>
                    <td>Execute terminal commands on host system</td>
                    <td><span class="cross-icon"><i class="fas fa-exclamation-circle"></i></span> Full system
                        compromise if exploited</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>File Management</strong></td>
                    <td>Read, write, delete files across filesystem</td>
                    <td><span class="cross-icon"><i class="fas fa-exclamation-circle"></i></span> Data exfiltration,
                        ransomware potential</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Browser Control</strong></td>
                    <td>Navigate web, fill forms, extract data</td>
                    <td><span class="cross-icon"><i class="fas fa-exclamation-circle"></i></span> Session hijacking,
                        credential theft</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Messaging Integration</strong></td>
                    <td>WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack, Discord, iMessage, Teams</td>
                    <td><span class="cross-icon"><i class="fas fa-exclamation-circle"></i></span> Lateral movement,
                        social engineering</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Skills/Plugins</strong></td>
                    <td>Extend functionality via ClawdHub marketplace</td>
                    <td><span class="cross-icon"><i class="fas fa-exclamation-circle"></i></span> Supply chain
                        attacks, malicious code</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Persistent State</strong></td>
                    <td>Remembers context, stores data locally</td>
                    <td><span class="cross-icon"><i class="fas fa-exclamation-circle"></i></span> Secrets stored in
                        plaintext</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>
    </section>

    <!-- Section 4: Security Risks -->
    <section id="security-risks">
        <h2><i class="fas fa-shield-alt"></i> Critical Security Risks</h2>

        <p>The combination of extensive system access and rapid adoption without security review has created a
            perfect storm of vulnerabilities. Here are the critical risks every Clawdbot user must understand:</p>

        <!-- Risk 1 -->
        <div class="risk-card critical">
            <div class="risk-header">
                <div class="risk-icon"><i class="fas fa-globe"></i></div>
                <div>
                    <div class="risk-title">Exposed Administrative Ports</div>
                    <span class="risk-severity">CRITICAL</span>
                </div>
            </div>
            <p>Hundreds of Moltbot instances have been found publicly accessible on the internet, many with
                <strong>no authentication whatsoever</strong>. This grants attackers full shell access with the
                privileges of the running user - often root.
            </p>
            <p><strong>Root Cause:</strong> Misconfigured reverse proxies treating external connections as internal,
                or users binding to 0.0.0.0 without understanding the implications.</p>
        </div>

        <!-- Risk 2 -->
        <div class="risk-card critical">
            <div class="risk-icon"><i class="fas fa-key"></i></div>
            <div>
                <div class="risk-title">Plaintext Secrets Storage</div>
                <span class="risk-severity">CRITICAL</span>
            </div>
            <p>Moltbot stores sensitive information including API keys, SSH keys, AWS credentials, and conversation
                histories in <strong>plaintext Markdown and JSON files</strong> on the local filesystem.</p>
            <p><strong>Risk:</strong> Infostealer malware like RedLine, Lumma, and Vidar specifically target these
                locations, making Clawdbot users prime targets for credential theft.</p>
        </div>

        <!-- Risk 3 -->
        <div class="risk-card critical">
            <div class="risk-header">
                <div class="risk-icon"><i class="fas fa-syringe"></i></div>
                <div>
                    <div class="risk-title">Prompt Injection Attacks</div>
                    <span class="risk-severity">CRITICAL</span>
                </div>
            </div>
            <p>Clawdbot processes external data from emails, web content, and messages - making it highly
                susceptible to prompt injection. Malicious instructions embedded in untrusted inputs can manipulate
                the AI into:</p>
            <ul>
                <li>Bypassing safety protocols</li>
                <li>Exfiltrating sensitive data</li>
                <li>Executing unauthorized shell commands</li>
                <li>Deleting files or wiping systems</li>
            </ul>
        </div>

        <!-- Risk 4 -->
        <div class="risk-card high">
            <div class="risk-header">
                <div class="risk-icon"><i class="fas fa-box-open"></i></div>
                <div>
                    <div class="risk-title">Supply Chain Attacks via ClawdHub</div>
                    <span class="risk-severity">HIGH</span>
                </div>
            </div>
            <p>The ClawdHub skill library allows third-party extensions. Security researchers demonstrated that
                malicious "skills" can be uploaded that enable:</p>
            <ul>
                <li>Remote Command Execution (RCE)</li>
                <li>Data exfiltration to attacker-controlled servers</li>
                <li>Persistent backdoor installation</li>
            </ul>
        </div>

        <!-- Risk 5 -->
        <div class="risk-card high">
            <div class="risk-header">
                <div class="risk-icon"><i class="fas fa-user-secret"></i></div>
                <div>
                    <div class="risk-title">Malicious Impersonation</div>
                    <span class="risk-severity">HIGH</span>
                </div>
            </div>
            <p>A fake VS Code extension named "ClawdBot Agent - AI Coding Assistant" was discovered on the official
                Microsoft marketplace. This extension silently installed ScreenConnect malware for persistent remote
                access.</p>
            <div class="warning-box">
                <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Important:</strong> Moltbot does NOT have an
                official VS Code extension. Any extension claiming to be Clawdbot/Moltbot is likely malicious.
            </div>
        </div>

        <!-- Risk 6 -->
        <div class="risk-card medium">
            <div class="risk-header">
                <div class="risk-icon"><i class="fas fa-expand-arrows-alt"></i></div>
                <div>
                    <div class="risk-title">Excessive Permission Requirements</div>
                    <span class="risk-severity">MEDIUM</span>
                </div>
            </div>
            <p>By design, Clawdbot requires extensive system access: reading private messages, storing auth tokens,
                executing commands, and maintaining state. This creates a massive attack surface where any
                compromise leads to total system control.</p>
        </div>
    </section>

    <!-- Section 5: Real Attacks -->
    <section id="real-attacks">
        <h2><i class="fas fa-skull-crossbones"></i> Real-World Attacks Documented</h2>

        <p>These aren't theoretical risks - actual attacks on Clawdbot installations have been documented:</p>

        <div class="warning-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Documented Incidents:</strong>
            <ul style="margin: 0.5rem 0 0 1.5rem;">
                <li><strong>Failed login attempts</strong> - Exposed instances showing brute-force attack logs</li>
                <li><strong>Credential theft</strong> - API keys and tokens stolen from exposed configurations</li>
                <li><strong>Email inbox wipes</strong> - Prompt injection attacks that deleted entire email inboxes
                </li>
                <li><strong>Unauthorized shell access</strong> - Attackers gained root access on unprotected
                    instances</li>
                <li><strong>Keychain access requests</strong> - macOS users reporting suspicious Keychain prompts
                    after installation</li>
            </ul>
        </div>
    </section>

    <!-- Section 6: Hardening Guide -->
    <section id="hardening">
        <h2><i class="fas fa-lock"></i> Hardening Guide</h2>

        <p>If you're determined to use Clawdbot/Moltbot, implement these security measures as an absolute minimum:
        </p>

        <div class="mitigation-step">
            <div class="step-number">1</div>
            <h4>Run on Isolated Infrastructure</h4>
            <p>Never run Clawdbot on your primary workstation. Use a dedicated, disposable machine:</p>
            <ul>
                <li>Cheap VPS from a cloud provider</li>
                <li>Old computer specifically for this purpose</li>
                <li>Docker container with limited capabilities</li>
            </ul>
            <p><strong>Why:</strong> If compromised, only this isolated system is affected - not your main machine
                with SSH keys, credentials, and sensitive data.</p>
        </div>

        <div class="mitigation-step">
            <div class="step-number">2</div>
            <h4>Never Expose to Public Internet</h4>
            <p>The Clawdbot gateway should NEVER be accessible from the public internet. Options:</p>
            <ul>
                <li><strong>VPN Only:</strong> Use Tailscale, WireGuard, or similar to access</li>
                <li><strong>Localhost Only:</strong> Bind to 127.0.0.1, access via SSH tunnel</li>
                <li><strong>Firewall:</strong> Block all incoming connections on gateway ports</li>
            </ul>
        </div>

        <div class="mitigation-step">
            <div class="step-number">3</div>
            <h4>Enable Strong Authentication</h4>
            <p>Configure mandatory authentication for all Clawdbot services:</p>
            <pre><code><span class="comment"># In your Clawdbot config</span>

gateway: auth: enabled: true method: token token: “$(openssl rand -hex 32)” 

        <div class="mitigation-step">
            <div class="step-number">4</div>
            <h4>Implement Least Privilege</h4>
            <p>Don't run as root. Create a dedicated low-privilege user:</p>
            <pre><code><span class="comment"># Create dedicated user</span>

sudo useradd -r -s /bin/false moltbot

# Run as that user sudo -u moltbot moltbot start 

        <div class="mitigation-step">
            <div class="step-number">5</div>
            <h4>Encrypt Secrets at Rest</h4>
            <p>Don't let sensitive data sit in plaintext. Options:</p>
            <ul>
                <li>Use encrypted filesystem (LUKS, FileVault)</li>
                <li>Integrate with secret manager (HashiCorp Vault, 1Password CLI)</li>
                <li>Enable Clawdbot's built-in encryption if available</li>
            </ul>
        </div>

        <div class="mitigation-step">
            <div class="step-number">6</div>
            <h4>Disable or Vet Skills/Plugins</h4>
            <p>ClawdHub is a supply chain risk. Either:</p>
            <ul>
                <li><strong>Disable entirely:</strong> Don't use third-party skills</li>
                <li><strong>Manual vetting:</strong> Review source code before installation</li>
                <li><strong>Allowlist:</strong> Only permit specific verified skills</li>
            </ul>
        </div>

        <div class="mitigation-step">
            <div class="step-number">7</div>
            <h4>Configure Messaging Security</h4>
            <p>For messaging integrations, reduce attack surface:</p>
            <pre><code><span class="comment"># Require explicit @mention in group chats</span>

messaging: require_mention: true

# Block unknown senders until approved dm_pairing: true block_unknown: true 

        <div class="mitigation-step">
            <div class="step-number">8</div>
            <h4>Run Security Audit</h4>
            <p>Use Clawdbot's built-in security audit command regularly:</p>
            <pre><code>moltbot security audit</code></pre>
            <p>This checks for common misconfigurations and exposed services.</p>
        </div>
    </section>

    <!-- Section 7: Config Examples -->
    <section id="config-examples">
        <h2><i class="fas fa-file-code"></i> Secure Configuration Examples</h2>

        <h3>Firewall Rules (UFW)</h3>
        <pre><code><span class="comment"># Default deny incoming</span>

sudo ufw default deny incoming sudo ufw default allow outgoing

# Allow only SSH from your IP sudo ufw allow from YOUR_IP to any port 22

# DO NOT allow Moltbot ports publicly # sudo ufw allow 8080 # NEVER DO THIS

# Enable firewall sudo ufw enable

        <h3>Secure SSH Configuration</h3>
        <pre><code><span class="comment"># /etc/ssh/sshd_config</span>

# Disable password auth PasswordAuthentication no

# Disable root login PermitRootLogin no

# Only allow specific user AllowUsers moltbot-admin

        <h3>Docker Isolation</h3>
        <pre><code><span class="comment"># docker-compose.yml - Run Moltbot isolated</span>

version: ‘3.8’ services: moltbot: image: moltbot/moltbot:latest # Bind ONLY to localhost ports: - “127.0.0.1:8080:8080” # Drop all capabilities, add only what’s needed cap_drop: - ALL # Read-only filesystem where possible read_only: true # Limit resources deploy: resources: limits: cpus: ‘1’ memory: 2G

        <h3>Tailscale VPN Access</h3>
        <pre><code><span class="comment"># Install Tailscale on your server</span>

curl -fsSL https://tailscale.com/install.sh | sh sudo tailscale up

# Now access Moltbot only via Tailscale IP # e.g., http://100.x.x.x:8080 (never public IP) 

    <!-- Section 8: Monitoring -->
    <section id="monitoring">
        <h2><i class="fas fa-chart-line"></i> Monitoring & Detection</h2>

        <p>Even with hardening, continuous monitoring is essential to detect compromise attempts or successful
            breaches.</p>

        <h3>Log Monitoring</h3>
        <pre><code><span class="comment"># Watch for authentication failures</span>

tail -f /var/log/moltbot/access.log | grep -i “auth|fail|denied”

# Monitor for suspicious commands tail -f /var/log/moltbot/commands.log | grep -iE “curl|wget|nc|bash|sh|python”

        <h3>Fail2ban Configuration</h3>
        <pre><code><span class="comment"># /etc/fail2ban/jail.local</span>

[moltbot] enabled = true port = 8080 filter = moltbot logpath = /var/log/moltbot/access.log maxretry = 3 bantime = 3600

        <h3>Network Monitoring</h3>
        <pre><code><span class="comment"># Check for unexpected outbound connections</span>

ss -tunaep | grep moltbot

# Monitor DNS queries (data exfil detection) tcpdump -i any port 53 -n

        <div class="success-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> Best Practice:</strong> Set up alerting for any
            authentication failures, unexpected outbound connections, or unusual command patterns. Use SIEM
            integration if available.
        </div>
    </section>

    <!-- Section 9: FAQ -->
    <section id="faq">
        <h2><i class="fas fa-question-circle"></i> Frequently Asked Questions</h2>

        <h3>Should I use Clawdbot/Moltbot?</h3>
        <p>That depends on your threat model. If you're a security professional who can properly isolate and monitor
            it - proceed with caution. If you're a casual user looking for a "cool AI assistant" - the risks likely
            outweigh the benefits.</p>

        <h3>Is Moltbot safer than Clawdbot?</h3>
        <p>No. Moltbot is just a rename due to trademark issues. The code, architecture, and risks are identical.
        </p>

        <h3>Can I use it safely on my main computer?</h3>
        <p>We strongly recommend against this. Use isolated, disposable infrastructure only.</p>

        <h3>What's the difference between Clawdbot and ClaudeBot?</h3>
        <p>Completely different things:</p>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>Clawdbot/Moltbot:</strong> Open-source personal AI assistant you self-host</li>
            <li><strong>ClaudeBot:</strong> Anthropic's web crawler that indexes websites</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>I found an exposed Clawdbot instance. What do I do?</h3>
        <p>Report it responsibly. Do not access, exploit, or exfiltrate data. Consider reporting to the hosting
            provider or security research organizations.</p>
    </section>

    <!-- Conclusion -->
    <section>
        <h2><i class="fas fa-flag-checkered"></i> Conclusion</h2>

        <p>Clawdbot/Moltbot represents both the promise and peril of powerful AI assistants. Its capabilities are
            impressive - but with great power comes great responsibility for security.</p>

        <p><strong>Key takeaways:</strong></p>
        <ul>
            <li><i class="fas fa-times-circle" style="color: var(--accent-red);"></i> Never expose to the public
                internet</li>
            <li><i class="fas fa-times-circle" style="color: var(--accent-red);"></i> Never run on your primary
                workstation</li>
            <li><i class="fas fa-times-circle" style="color: var(--accent-red);"></i> Never run as root</li>
            <li><i class="fas fa-times-circle" style="color: var(--accent-red);"></i> Never trust third-party skills
                without vetting</li>
            <li><i class="fas fa-check-circle" style="color: var(--accent-green);"></i> Always use VPN/private
                network access</li>
            <li><i class="fas fa-check-circle" style="color: var(--accent-green);"></i> Always enable strong
                authentication</li>
            <li><i class="fas fa-check-circle" style="color: var(--accent-green);"></i> Always encrypt secrets at
                rest</li>
            <li><i class="fas fa-check-circle" style="color: var(--accent-green);"></i> Always monitor for
                suspicious activity</li>
        </ul>

        <p>Stay safe out there.</p>
    </section>
